text: 23-year-old female. The patient presents with knee pain that started yesterday and has been steadily worsening. She was advised at her last physical exam that weight loss could be beneficial for her health.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see that you are a 23-year-old female with knee pain following volleyball activities involving pivoting and twisting. Can you tell me if you heard or felt a "pop" at the moment of injury, and have you experienced any swelling or instability in the knee since then?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Knee pain, specifically over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. I also have Recent weight loss attempt, Increased physical activity.

speaker: Doctor
text: The location of your pain on the medial tibial plateau is very specific and less typical for a standard ACL injury. Do you experience sharp pain when going up or down stairs or when squatting, and is the pain reproducible when I press on the joint line?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), currently managed with oral contraceptive pills. Social history: Has recently joined a volleyball team.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that history. Given the pain is localized to the medial tibial plateau rather than the patellar tendon, I am concerned about a meniscal issue rather than a simple overuse injury. Can you tell me if the knee has ever locked, caught, or given way unexpectedly since the pain started?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any fever, recent injuries, swelling or discoloration of the knee, or previous similar complaints.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since you deny swelling, locking, or instability, a meniscal tear is less likely, so I suspect patellofemoral pain syndrome from your increased activity. I will order an X-ray to rule out any bony abnormalities or stress fractures. REQUEST TEST: Knee_X-Ray
